overview.title: Concepts recap
overview.lede: Everything below was covered in the lecture. Read it as a checklist: if any card makes you pause, that is the part to review before the practical lesson.

quiz.title: Quick check
quiz.lede: Five questions. No score is stored. This is just to see what stuck.

questions.question: What is a token, technically?
options: A file stored inside a user’s wallet
A row in a ledger that says which account controls how much of an asset
A copy of a coin sent from one computer to another
A smart contract, always
questions.explanation: Nothing is ever “inside” a wallet. A token is an entry in a shared ledger: an amount attributed to an account. Your wallet only holds the private key that lets you authorise changes to that entry.

questions.question: What does “tokenization” mean?
options: Encrypting sensitive data so it cannot be read
Converting a currency into another currency
Representing a right or an asset as a transferable ledger entry
Splitting a payment into smaller instalments
questions.explanation: Careful: the word also exists in payment security, where “tokenization” means replacing a card number with a surrogate value. In blockchain, it means representing ownership of something (a dollar, a bond, a building, a concert seat) as a ledger entry that can be transferred and settled.

questions.question: Which of these is fungible?
options: The deed to a specific apartment
Seat 14B on a specific flight
One USDC out of a million USDC
A one-of-a-kind artwork
questions.explanation: Fungible means interchangeable: any one unit is as good as any other, and units can be split and merged. Non-fungible means each unit has an identity that matters: a seat number, a deed, a serial.

questions.question: On Stellar, what does a trustline do?
options: It proves the issuer is a licensed company
It records that an account is willing to hold a specific asset, and up to what limit
It transfers the token to the account
It locks the token so it cannot be sold
questions.explanation: A trustline is an explicit opt-in stored on the receiving account: “I accept CODE from this issuer, up to this limit.” Without one, a payment in that asset simply fails.

questions.question: Why do most other chains not have trustlines?
options: Their tokens are safer by design
They track balances inside each token contract instead of on the account, so anyone can push a balance to any address
They charge a fee that makes it unnecessary
They do have trustlines, under another name
questions.explanation: On an EVM-style chain the balance lives in the token contract’s own mapping, so a sender can write into it without the recipient’s consent, which is why address books fill up with unsolicited scam tokens. Stellar puts the asset entry on the account itself, so it requires consent and a reserve.

fungibility.title: Fungible and non-fungible
fungibility.lede: The difference is not technical sophistication. It is whether units have an identity.

fungible.title: Fungible token
points: Every unit is interchangeable with every other unit
Divisible: you can send 0.37 of one
Balances merge: 3 + 5 is just 8
Priced per unit
fungible.examples: Currencies, stablecoins, shares of one class, loyalty points, carbon credits

nonFungible.title: Non-fungible token
points: Each unit has its own identifier and its own history
Not divisible: half a ticket is nothing
Balances do not merge: two NFTs stay two distinct things
Priced per item
nonFungible.examples: Property deeds, event tickets with a seat, diplomas, invoices, artwork

metadata.title: What metadata a token carries
metadata.lede: Metadata is what turns a number in a ledger into something a human can recognise. Some of it lives on chain; a lot of it does not, and knowing which is which is a security skill.

fungibleRows.meaning: The short symbol, 1–12 alphanumeric characters on Stellar (USDC, EURC, MYTOKEN)
The account that created it. This is the real identity of the token. The code alone is not unique
How finely it divides. Every classic Stellar asset uses 7 decimal places
How much has been issued. On Stellar it is derived: the sum of every holder’s balance
Whether the issuer must approve holders, can freeze them, or can claw tokens back
Published by the issuer in a stellar.toml file at their home domain

nonFungibleRows.meaning: The identifier of this one item inside the collection
The address that currently controls it
Which contract minted it, the equivalent of the issuer
A pointer to the JSON describing the item. On chain it is only the pointer
The JSON the URI resolves to. If it is hosted on a normal web server, the owner of that server can change it

callout.title: The thing to remember
callout.body: Anyone can issue an asset with the code USDC. What makes the real one real is the issuer address. Wallets and explorers show both. Always check the issuer, never the symbol alone.

assetTypes.title: The three kinds of asset on Stellar
assetTypes.lede: Stellar is unusual here: issuing a token is a built-in ledger feature, not something you write a program for. Smart contracts are an addition on top, not the foundation.

rows.what: The network’s own currency. It pays transaction fees and backs the minimum balance every account must keep.
rows.use: Fees, reserves, being the bridge asset in path payments

rows.what: A code plus an issuer account, issued with a plain payment operation. No program, no deployment. It is a ledger primitive.
rows.use: Stablecoins, tokenized deposits, loyalty points, anything that behaves like currency

rows.what: A built-in smart-contract wrapper around a classic asset, exposing the standard SEP-41 token interface at a contract address.
rows.use: Letting Soroban contracts hold and move an existing asset: DeFi, escrow, vaults

sacNote.title: SAC is a wrapper, not a second token
sacNote.body: The classic asset and its SAC are the same asset with the same balances. The contract address is just a second doorway into it, so that a smart contract can call transfer() instead of submitting a classic payment. Its address is derived from the asset and the network, so it is known before it is even deployed.

trustlines.title: Trustlines: Stellar’s consent step
trustlines.lede: This is the part that surprises people coming from other chains, and it is worth understanding properly because it explains an entire class of scams that Stellar does not have.
trustlines.howBody: Before an account can receive an asset, it submits a ChangeTrust operation: “I accept CODE issued by G…, up to this limit.” That creates a trustline: a sub-entry on the account holding the balance, the limit, and the authorization state. Paying an account with no trustline fails outright with op_no_trust.
trustlines.costBody: Each trustline raises the account’s minimum XLM balance by 0.5 XLM. That XLM is not spent. It is locked while the trustline exists, and released when you remove it. This is the reserve that makes spam expensive.
trustlines.whyOthersTitle: Why other chains don’t do this
trustlines.whyOthersBody: On an EVM-style chain, balances live inside each token contract’s own mapping. A sender writes into that mapping directly, so anyone can push any token to any address without asking. That is why wallets there fill with unsolicited “airdrops” that are really phishing bait. Stellar stores the asset entry on the account itself, so the ledger cannot record a balance the account never agreed to hold.
trustlines.tradeoffBody: Consent costs a step. Every wallet, exchange and anchor has to build “add trustline” into onboarding, and each one locks a little XLM. Stellar took that friction deliberately: cleaner balances, no forced tokens, and an issuer that can be required to authorise each holder, which is exactly what a regulated stablecoin needs.

flowSteps.title: Issuer exists
flowSteps.body: An ordinary account. Nothing marks it as an issuer until it sends its first payment.

flowSteps.title: Holder opts in
flowSteps.body: The holder signs ChangeTrust for CODE:ISSUER with a limit. 0.5 XLM of reserve is locked.

flowSteps.title: Issuer may authorise
flowSteps.body: Only if the asset has AUTH_REQUIRED set. That is the compliance path for regulated assets.

flowSteps.title: Issuer pays
flowSteps.body: A payment from the issuing account creates the tokens. Supply grows as they leave.

flowSteps.title: Tokens return to burn
flowSteps.body: A payment back to the issuer destroys them. An issuer never holds a balance of its own asset.

explorer.title: Reading an explorer
explorer.lede: An explorer is a read-only window on the ledger. You will use one after every step of the practical lesson, so learn what to look at.
explorer.whatToCheck: What to check on an asset page
checkItems: The issuer address, not just the code
How many accounts hold a trustline for it
Total supply, and whether the issuer is locked (can it print more?)
The home domain and whether a stellar.toml is actually published there
The authorization flags: can the issuer freeze or claw back your balance?

stablecoin.title: How a stablecoin is issued
stablecoin.lede: This is Circle’s USDC loop. Step through it and watch where the dollars go, when tokens are created, and what keeps one USDC worth one dollar.
stablecoin.hint: Use the arrows, or the ← → keys.

steps.title: A stablecoin is a claim on a dollar
steps.body: A stablecoin is a token whose price is meant to stay pegged to something stable, almost always the US dollar. It is not stable because the code says so. It is stable because the issuer promises that one token can always be exchanged for one dollar, and holds the dollars to make that promise good.
points: The peg is a redemption promise, not a technical property
Fiat-backed is the model used by USDC and USDT: one token, one real dollar held in reserve
Other designs exist too: crypto-overcollateralised (DAI), and algorithmic ones with no reserves at all (which is how UST collapsed in 2022)

callout.title: Why anyone wants this
callout.body: You get the settlement of a blockchain (final in seconds, open all night, cheap across borders) while still counting in dollars. That is why stablecoins settle more value on Stellar than anything else on the network.

steps.title: Opening a Circle Mint account
steps.body: New USDC only enters existence through Circle, and only for institutions. A business applies for a Circle Mint account and goes through KYB, sanctions screening and ongoing AML monitoring before it can mint or redeem anything.
points: Circle Mint is for exchanges, banks, institutional traders and large businesses, not individuals
Everyone else buys USDC that already exists, from an exchange or an on-ramp partner
That distinction matters: the primary market (mint and redeem at exactly 1:1) is small and gated; the secondary market where you and I buy is large and open

callout.title: So you never “mint” USDC
callout.body: When you buy USDC on an exchange you receive tokens that already exist. The supply only changes when a Mint account holder deposits or redeems.

steps.title: Dollars arrive by wire
steps.body: The business wires USD from its own bank to Circle. Circle credits their Mint account with a dollar balance. Notice what has not happened yet: no token exists. This is still an ordinary bank transfer between two ordinary bank accounts.
points: The deposit is fiat, settled on traditional banking rails
The Mint account balance is a liability Circle owes the customer, denominated in USD
USDC supply is unchanged. The ledger has not been touched

callout.title: Watch the two bars
callout.body: Dollars held by Circle just went up. USDC in circulation did not. They will only match again after the next step.

steps.title: Minting: dollars become tokens
steps.body: The business requests USDC against its dollar balance, names a blockchain and gives a wallet address. Circle mints exactly that amount on that chain and sends it. The dollars move into reserves; the tokens move to the customer. One dollar in, one token out.
points: The customer chooses the chain: Stellar, Ethereum, Solana, Base and others are all the same USDC
Total USDC supply increases by exactly the amount minted
The whole issuance operation is a single on-chain transaction, publicly visible, forever

callout.title: The invariant
callout.body: From this moment the two bars match again. Every USDC in existence corresponds to a dollar of reserves. Keeping that true is the entire job of a fiat-backed stablecoin issuer.

steps.title: Where the dollars actually sit
steps.body: The reserves are not a vault of cash. The majority is invested in the Circle Reserve Fund (ticker USDXX), an SEC-registered 2a-7 government money market fund managed by BlackRock and custodied at BNY Mellon. It holds short-dated US Treasuries and overnight Treasury repurchase agreements. The remainder is cash at regulated banks so redemptions can settle immediately.
points: Managed by BlackRock, custodied at BNY Mellon, not by Circle itself
Portfolio holdings are published daily by BlackRock, and Circle publishes a monthly reserve attestation by a Big Four firm (Deloitte)
Short-dated government paper is chosen because it can be sold fast without a loss. Liquidity matters more than yield when everyone might redeem at once

callout.title: This is the risk that actually matters
callout.body: A fiat-backed stablecoin’s real risk is not the smart contract. It is whether the reserves exist, are liquid, and are held somewhere safe. In March 2023 USDC briefly traded at $0.87 because $3.3bn of its cash sat at Silicon Valley Bank when the bank failed. The peg recovered the moment the deposits were guaranteed. Read attestations, not marketing.

steps.title: Who earns the interest
steps.body: Treasury bills pay interest. On tens of billions of dollars of reserves, that is a very large income, and it goes to the issuer, not to the holder. This is the business model: you hand over a dollar, you get back a token that pays you nothing, and the issuer keeps the yield.
points: Holding USDC earns you no interest. The token itself has no yield
In the US, the GENIUS Act explicitly forbids payment stablecoin issuers from paying interest to holders
Circle shares a large part of that revenue with distribution partners, most visibly Coinbase, which is paid for USDC held on its platform
Any “USDC yield” you are offered comes from somewhere else (lending it out, a DeFi protocol, an exchange promotion) and carries that party’s risk, not Circle’s

callout.title: The exam question
callout.body: If a stablecoin is fully backed and pays no interest, why would anyone hold one? Because they want dollars that settle on a blockchain: instantly, globally, at any hour. They are paying for settlement, not for return.

steps.title: Circulation, and what holds the peg
steps.body: Once minted, USDC moves like any other token: wallet to wallet, onto exchanges, into DeFi, across chains. Circle does not control where it goes. On the open market its price is set by supply and demand, so it can drift from a dollar. What pulls it back is arbitrage.
points: If USDC trades at $0.995, an institution buys it cheaply and redeems it at Circle for a full dollar, pocketing the difference, and buying pressure pushes the price back up
If it trades at $1.005, they mint new USDC at par and sell it into the market, and supply pressure pushes the price back down
The peg therefore depends on redemption being reliable and fast. When people doubt they can redeem, the arbitrage stops and the peg slips

callout.title: Why the primary market matters
callout.body: Mint and redeem are gated to institutions, but everyone benefits: those institutions are the arbitrageurs whose profit motive keeps the price you pay near one dollar.

steps.title: Redemption and the burn
steps.body: The loop closes. A Mint account holder sends USDC back to Circle and asks for dollars. Circle destroys the tokens (“burning” them) and wires the dollars back from reserves. Supply falls by exactly the amount burned, and the reserves fall with it.
points: Burning removes the tokens from circulation permanently; they are not resold
Reserves shrink in step, so the 1:1 backing holds on the way down too
This is why USDC supply falls in bear markets: people are redeeming, not selling into a void

callout.title: The whole model in one line
callout.body: Mint = dollars in, tokens out. Redeem = tokens in, dollars out. The issuer’s only job is to make sure those two are always exactly equal.

steps.title: The same loop, in Stellar terms
steps.body: USDC on Stellar is not a smart contract. It is a plain classic asset: code USDC, issued by one Circle account. The whole mint-and-burn loop maps onto operations you are about to use yourself in the next lesson.
points: Minting = a payment operation from the issuing account. The tokens come into existence as they leave it
Burning = a payment back to the issuing account. An issuer never holds a balance of its own asset, so receiving it destroys it
Holding = a trustline. Before any wallet can receive USDC on Stellar it must opt in to CODE:ISSUER
Compliance = issuer flags. Authorization required, revocable, and clawback are protocol features, not custom code

callout.title: Your turn
callout.body: In the next lesson you do exactly this: create an issuer, add a trustline from your own wallet, and mint a supply into it. The only difference is the size of the reserve behind it.

case1.title: Mission 01: Read the wallet
case1.lede: One address, nothing else. By the end of this mission you can open any Stellar wallet in the explorer and say what it holds, who created it and everything it has ever done, with no tools beyond a browser.

manual.title: Field guide: what an account page is showing you
manual.lede: Stellar Expert puts everything about a wallet on one page. Once you know what each box is for, reading a wallet takes about a minute.

items.body: When the wallet was created and by whom, its home domain, how many signatures it needs, whether it is locked. Half of this mission's answers are in this one box.
items.where: Account page → Summary box, top left

items.body: One tile per asset: the amount on top, the token code underneath. XLM is the network's own currency; every other tile is a token the wallet deliberately opted in to hold.
items.where: Account page → Account Balances box, top right

items.body: Everything the wallet has ever done, written as sentences: “GAE4…MOP3 sent 450 VKUSD to GBX4…FHWC”. Newest first, so scroll to the bottom and you reach the moment it was born.
What the wallet says about itself: a website it claims, plus free-form notes it wrote onto the ledger. Useful, and self-declared: a claim, not a proof.
items.where: Account page → Summary and Data Entries

items.body: Click any token code, anywhere, and you land on that token's own page: who issued it, how much exists, how many wallets hold it. Mission 02 lives on this page.
items.where: Click a token code anywhere in the explorer

layers.title: Transaction, operation, ledger
layers.lede: Three words the explorer uses constantly. Five minutes on them now saves a lot of confusion later.

items.name: Transaction
items.body: One signed submission to the network. In the explorer, each History row is a transaction (plus its fee line). A single transaction can carry up to 100 separate actions.

items.name: Operation
items.body: One action inside that transaction: a payment, opening a trustline, a settings change. A History row can expand into several of them, which is why “one transaction” never means “one payment”.

items.name: Ledger
items.body: Roughly every five seconds the network agrees on a new page of the book containing every transaction from that moment. Once agreed it is never edited and never deleted, not even by the wallet's owner.

case1.briefLede: A real wallet on Stellar testnet, set up for this workshop. Open it in the explorer and answer the six questions. Nothing here needs guessing: every answer is visible on the page.
case1.evidenceHint: Paste this into the Stellar Expert search box, or use the button. Keep the explorer open in a second tab while you work through the questions.

creator.prompt: Which account created this wallet and paid for the XLM it started with?
creator.hint: The Summary box, top left of the account page. One of its lines names the account that created this one.
creator.explain: Every Stellar wallet is created by another account, which hands over its starting balance. The explorer reads that from the very first entry in the wallet's history and prints it as “Created by”. A wallet's origin can never be hidden.

holdings.prompt: How many assets other than XLM does the wallet hold?
holdings.hint: The Account Balances box. XLM is the network's own currency and does not count; each remaining tile is one token.
holdings.explain: Two tiles, two tokens. Each one locks 0.5 XLM of reserve, which is part of why the wallet holds less XLM than it was created with.

issuer.hint: In Account Balances, click that token's tile. The page that opens starts with “Issued by” and an address.
issuer.explain: A token's identity on Stellar is the pair (code, issuer). The code alone means nothing, since anyone may issue a token called {code}. The issuer account is what makes it unique, and it is the only account that can create more.

balance.prompt: How many {code} does the wallet hold?
balance.hint: The number printed on that token's tile in Account Balances.
balance.explain: Amounts on Stellar always carry seven decimal places, so the explorer may show this as 3,250 and the token page as 3,250.0000000. Same number.

spendTo.prompt: The wallet sent {code} to exactly one other address. Which one?
spendTo.hint: Scroll down to History and read the rows as sentences: who sent what to whom. You want the row where this wallet is the sender of that token.
spendTo.explain: Direction is what people most often get backwards. The explorer writes it out in words, “sent … to …”, so read the row rather than guessing from the amount.

homeDomain.prompt: What home domain has this wallet published?
homeDomain.hint: The first line of the Summary box.
homeDomain.explain: A home domain points at a website that is supposed to publish who owns the wallet. It is self-declared: the wallet claims a domain, and only that website can confirm the claim.

debrief.title: Walkthrough: how the explorer knows all this
debrief.lede: The same boxes you just used, now from the bottom up: where the data comes from, and which part of the page answers which question.
debrief.diagramTitle: An account page, and where each box comes from

steps.title: The explorer is a reader, not a source
steps.body: The Stellar network is a few hundred independent computers that agree, about every five seconds, on a new page of a shared book. That book is public and cannot be rewritten. Stellar Expert simply reads it back and lays it out nicely. It invents nothing.
points: Anyone can read the same data, with no account and no permission
Two explorers may show different names and labels, never different numbers
Nothing can be deleted afterwards, not by the wallet owner, not by anyone

callout.title: Labels are not ledger data
callout.body: When an explorer prints “Circle USDC” next to a token, that name was added by the explorer. The network itself only knows a code and an issuing account.

steps.title: One page holds almost the whole answer
steps.body: Everything above the history (balances, home domain, notes, the creation date and the creator) is the wallet's own entry in that shared book. Five of your six answers were on this single screen.
points: The XLM balance is the network's own currency, used to pay the tiny fees
Every token the wallet accepts locks 0.5 XLM of reserve, so some XLM is never spendable
“Last year activity” and “Total payments” give you the size of the wallet at a glance

callout.title: Try it
callout.body: Open the page again and read it top to bottom: address, home domain, created by, balances. That order is a good habit for any wallet you ever look at.

steps.title: A wallet has to accept a token before it can receive it
steps.body: A token balance is not stored inside the wallet. It is a separate line, called a trustline, which the wallet opens on purpose, recording the token, the issuer, the balance and a limit the holder chooses.
points: Nobody can push an unwanted token into a Stellar wallet
The limit is the maximum the holder agrees to hold; the issuer cannot raise it
In History you can see this as “established trustline to …” before the first payment arrives

callout.title: Opt-in by design
callout.body: On most blockchains anyone can send you any token, and wallets fill up with junk. On Stellar the holder pays 0.5 XLM of reserve and agrees first, so token spam is priced out.

steps.title: History reads like sentences
steps.body: Every row says who did what to whom, in words. That is the whole skill: read the rows, keep track of the direction, and ignore the fee lines in between.
points: Newest first, so to see how a wallet started, scroll all the way to the bottom
The explorer keeps loading more as you scroll; don't conclude anything from the first screen
One row can hide several actions at once, so open the arrow on the right when a row looks busy

callout.title: The classic mistake
callout.body: Reading the first few rows and deciding that is all of it. Keep scrolling until nothing more loads.

steps.title: What the wallet says about itself
steps.body: The home domain and the data entries are the only places a wallet can write free text about itself. They are useful, and they are claims rather than verified facts.
points: A home domain points at a website; that website is where ownership is supposed to be published
Data entries are notes the wallet wrote onto the ledger itself
Anyone can claim any domain, and a claim does not prove itself

callout.title: Never trust a label
callout.body: A wallet claiming a bank's domain proves nothing until you visit that bank's website and find this exact address published there.

case2.title: Mission 02: Follow the airdrop
case2.lede: One token address, and nothing else. Find who issued it, who handed it out, who received it, and whether more can still be created. That sequence is how anyone checks a token before trusting it.

toolkit.title: Three questions, always in this order
toolkit.lede: Whatever the token, you ask the same three things: what is it exactly, how much of it exists, and who is holding it. Answer them in order and the rest of the picture assembles itself.

items.name: Identity: what exactly is this token?
items.body: A token on Stellar is a code plus the account that issued it. The code alone identifies nothing: any number of accounts can issue a token called USDC. Always get to an issuer address before you say anything else about it.
items.where: Search box at the top → paste the address

items.name: Supply: how much exists, and can more appear?
items.body: The supply is everything the issuer has handed out and not taken back. Whether more can appear is a separate question, and the asset page answers it in one line.

items.name: Distribution: who holds it, and how did they get it?
items.body: Follow the payments outward from the issuer. The first stop is usually a treasury account; the next are the real holders. The number of wallets holding a token is not the number of wallets that were paid.

case2.briefLede: You get a token address and nothing else. Eight questions; every answer is visible in the explorer, and one of them is a trap that catches professionals.
case2.evidenceHint: A token address on Stellar testnet. Paste it into the Stellar Expert search box. The page it opens will tell you what token this is.

issuer.hint: Paste the address into the search box. The page says “Contract from asset” and names the token; click the token to open its page, which begins with “Issued by”.
issuer.explain: A token address on Stellar always maps back to exactly one code and one issuing account. Watch out: on testnet a second account issues a token with this very same code, and it is a completely different token.

supply.prompt: How many units of this token exist in total?
supply.hint: On the token's page, the Summary box has a line called Total supply.
supply.explain: Stellar has no separate supply counter. The supply is simply everything the issuer has handed out and not received back, added up from the holders, so the number can never disagree with the balances.

treasury.prompt: The issuer sent the entire supply to one account, all at once. Which account?
treasury.hint: Open the issuer's account page and read its History. An issuer that only ever handed out its token once has almost no history to read.
treasury.explain: Keeping issuance and distribution in two different accounts is standard practice: the issuer hands the supply over once and is then locked away, while a distributor account does the day-to-day sending.

recipients.prompt: How many wallets received the airdrop directly from the distributor?
recipients.hint: Open the distributor's account page and count the History rows where it sends the token out. They are not all in one place, so keep scrolling.
recipients.explain: Six wallets, handed out in two batches of four and two. Meanwhile the token's page reports eight holders: the distributor itself, plus one wallet that was never airdropped and got its tokens another way. Holders are not recipients.

whale.prompt: Which wallet received the largest airdrop?
whale.hint: Compare the amounts in those same History rows. The token page's “Asset Holders” tab also ranks wallets by balance, but careful: the wallet at the top of it was never airdropped at all.
whale.explain: Concentration is the first thing anyone measures: this single wallet got more than a third of everything handed out. For a real token that one number decides whether one holder can move the whole market.

forward.prompt: One of the six recipients immediately passed part of its airdrop to another wallet. Which wallet received it?
forward.hint: The token page → “Asset Holders” tab lists more wallets than the airdrop paid. Find the one that is not on the airdrop list, open it, and see who sent it the token.
forward.explain: This is why airdrop numbers age badly: the recipient list is a photograph, and it starts going out of date the moment the tokens are sent. Anything serious has to follow the second hop, and then the third.

mintMore.prompt: Can the issuer still create more of this token?
options: Yes, an issuer can always create more at any time
No, the issuer's key was destroyed after handing out the supply, so it can never act again
Only if the holders agree to it
mintMore.hint: The token's page → Summary → “Issuer account lock status”.
mintMore.explain: Locking the issuer is how a fixed supply is proven on Stellar rather than promised. The account can never sign anything again, so the supply is frozen for good, and it is one of very few things on the network that cannot be undone.

lookalike.prompt: One of the six recipients also holds a second token with exactly the same code. Which account issued that look-alike?
lookalike.hint: Open the six recipient wallets one by one. Exactly one of them shows two balance tiles with the same token code. Click the unfamiliar tile and read its “Issued by” line.
lookalike.explain: Two completely different tokens that share a name. The ledger has no idea they look alike, and the imitation even publishes a more official-sounding website than the real one. Checking the issuer address is the only defence, and it costs five seconds.

debrief.title: Walkthrough: anatomy of an airdrop
debrief.lede: Seven steps from a bare token address to a full picture of who holds what, with the page to open at each step.
debrief.diagramTitle: The airdrop, from issuance to the second hop

steps.title: An address that turns out to be a token
steps.body: Addresses starting with C are contracts. This one is the standard token contract that Stellar builds for a classic asset, so its page names the token it stands for: one code, one issuing account.
points: The contract page says “Contract from asset” and links straight to the token
The token page links back the other way, under “Soroban Contract”
Balances in ordinary wallets are unaffected, since it is the same token seen through a second door

callout.title: You have met this before
callout.body: It is the contract the issuing lesson creates. Same thing, now seen from the reading side.

steps.title: A token's name proves nothing
steps.body: Two accounts on testnet issue a token with this code. They are different tokens with different issuers, different supplies and different holders. The network has no idea they share a name.
points: Always write down the code and the issuer together; the code alone is not an identifier
The imitation here even publishes a more official-looking website than the genuine issuer
Wallets and explorers add trust badges themselves, and those badges are not part of the ledger

callout.title: How people actually lose money
callout.body: A convincing website, a familiar token code, and one tap to accept it. The issuer address is the only part of that story anyone can check.

steps.title: Tokens are created by being sent
steps.body: The issuer created the entire supply by sending it to the distributor. On Stellar a token comes into existence as it leaves the issuing account. There is no separate “create tokens” button.
points: Everything the issuer has sent out and not got back is the supply, and that is what the token page reports
Sending tokens back to the issuer destroys them again
So an issuer's own history is the shortest and most revealing history you will read

callout.title: Why this is tidy
callout.body: There is no separate supply number that could disagree with the balances. The balances are the supply.

steps.title: Two transactions, six payments
steps.body: The distributor paid six wallets across two transactions. Every recipient had already accepted the token, which is why the tokens could arrive at all.
points: One transaction can carry up to 100 payments, so counting transactions tells you nothing about the number of recipients
Each recipient's acceptance costs them 0.5 XLM of reserve, which real airdrops usually fund first
Counting the distinct destination addresses is the only reliable way to size an airdrop

callout.title: The Stellar difference
callout.body: An airdrop list on Stellar is also a consent list: every wallet on it had agreed to hold the token before it was paid.

steps.title: The list starts going stale immediately
steps.body: One recipient passed part of its share to a wallet that was never in the airdrop. There are now more holders than recipients, and the gap widens every day.
points: The token page shows eight holders against six airdropped wallets
This is where fraud analysis starts: recipients that instantly funnel everything into one address
Following it properly means opening every recipient, not just the distributor

callout.title: Never report holders as recipients
callout.body: They answer different questions, and the difference between them only grows with time.

steps.title: The issuer threw away its key
steps.body: After handing out the supply, the issuer disabled its own key. The account can never sign anything again, so no more of this token can ever exist.
points: The token page states it in one line: issuer account lock status
Any rules the issuer wanted (freezing, reclaiming) must be set before locking; afterwards nothing can change
A locked issuer is a fact you can check, not a promise in a whitepaper

callout.title: What to check on any token
callout.body: Issuer address, issuer lock status, home domain, and whether that website really lists this issuer. In that order, before you buy anything.

steps.title: The five-minute check you can now run on any token
steps.body: Everything in this mission works the same way on the real network, for a token someone sends you at three in the morning. It is five clicks.
points: Open the token page: who issued it, how much exists, how many hold it, is the issuer locked
Open the issuer: how old is it, what has it done, does its website really name this token
Open the top holders: is one wallet holding most of the supply, and where did it get it

callout.title: Where to go next
callout.body: Do the same walk on a token you have actually heard of, on the real network. The layout of the pages is identical.

further.title: Take it further
further.lede: Three harder hunts on the same token, if you finish early.
items: Write out every holder with its balance and check that they add up to the total supply.
Open the look-alike token's issuer and compare its website with the genuine one. Which looks more trustworthy, and what does that tell you?
The distributor still holds most of the supply. How much exactly, and who would have to agree before it could move?

tools.label: Stellar Expert on the real network, to run the same check on real tokens
What Stellar is, in plain language

case3.title: Mission 03: The wallet that cannot spend
case3.lede: A customer wallet holding 10,000 tokens it is not allowed to move. Work out what the token is, who controls it, why this wallet is stuck, and what the same issuer has done to two other customers. Same explorer, no lecturer.

homework.title: How to hand this in
homework.body: Work on your own. Write down your eight answers and, next to each one, the page where you found it. Open the walkthrough at the bottom only after you have answered everything: it is the answer key, and it explains what all of this means for anyone holding a token like this.

powers.title: What a regulated issuer can do to your balance
powers.lede: A token can be issued with rules attached. These three are chosen by the issuer once, before anybody holds the token, and the explorer prints them on the token's page for everyone to read.

items.name: Approval before holding
items.body: With this rule on, a wallet cannot receive the token until the issuer approves that specific wallet. Agreeing to hold it is not enough; someone at the issuer has to say yes. This is how a bank keeps unverified customers out.
items.where: Token page → Asset authorization flags → required

items.name: Freezing a balance
items.body: The issuer can take that approval away again later. The balance stays in the wallet and everyone can still see it, but it cannot move at all. The explorer marks it with a small padlock next to the token.
items.where: Account page → Account Balances → padlock on the tile

items.name: Taking tokens back
items.body: The strongest one. The issuer can remove tokens from a wallet without the owner signing anything. It exists for court orders and stolen funds, and it has to be switched on before anyone holds the token.
items.where: Token page → Asset authorization flags → clawback_enabled

case3.briefLede: One customer wallet on Stellar testnet. Eight questions, all of them answerable by clicking around the explorer. The last one is harder than the rest.
case3.evidenceHint: A customer of a bank that issues its own token on Stellar. Open it in the explorer and start with the balances box.

issuer.prompt: Which account issued the token this wallet is holding?
issuer.hint: In Account Balances, click the token tile. The page that opens starts with Issued by and an address.
issuer.explain: Identity first, always. A token is a code plus the account that issued it, and everything else in this mission is something that one account decided to do.

frozen.prompt: There is a small padlock next to the token balance. What does it mean?
options: The wallet has run out of XLM to pay transaction fees
The issuer has taken away this wallet's permission to use the token
The tokens were sent to the wrong address by mistake
frozen.hint: Read the newest row in this wallet's History. The issuer did something to this wallet shortly after the wallet last spent.
frozen.explain: The balance is still there and everyone can see it, but it cannot move. Nothing is broken in the wallet: the issuer simply took back the permission it granted when the wallet first accepted the token.

payer.prompt: Which account paid the 12,000 tokens into this wallet?
payer.hint: History again, the row that says sent 12,000 to this wallet.
payer.explain: Banks rarely pay customers from the issuing account itself. A separate distribution account does the daily work, so the address that pays you is usually not the address that created the token.

supply.prompt: How many of these tokens exist in total?
supply.hint: Open the token page and read Total supply in the Summary box.
supply.explain: Frozen tokens still count. They exist, they are simply not allowed to move, which is why this number is larger than what the unfrozen wallets add up to.

mintMore.prompt: Can this issuer create more of the token?
options: No, its key was destroyed after the first issuance
Yes, the issuer account is unlocked and has already issued twice
Only if every holder agrees to it
mintMore.hint: The token page says it in one line: issuer account lock status. Then count how many times the issuer has sent tokens out in its History.
mintMore.explain: This is the opposite of the token in mission 02. Neither is wrong by itself: a bank that has to match tokens to real deposits needs to keep issuing, while a fixed-supply token proves scarcity by throwing the key away. What matters is knowing which one you are holding.

clawback.prompt: The issuer took 5,000 tokens back from one customer. Which wallet lost them?
clawback.hint: Open the issuer's own account page and read its History. One row says clawed back.
clawback.explain: No signature from the owner, no warning, no way to refuse. The power was written into the token before anybody held it, and the explorer states it in plain words.

burn.prompt: One customer sent tokens back to the issuer. How many?
burn.hint: Still on the issuer's History: find the row where a customer sends tokens to the issuer rather than the other way round.
burn.explain: Tokens that arrive at the issuing account stop existing. On Stellar that is what burning is, and the total supply falls by exactly that amount.

topHolder.prompt: Apart from the distributor, which wallet holds the most of this token today?
topHolder.hint: The token page has an Asset Holders tab. Ignore the account sitting on most of the supply, that one is the distributor.
topHolder.explain: Holder lists are the fastest way to see who actually has the money, and they are public for every token and every wallet on Stellar.

debrief.title: Walkthrough: a token with rules attached
debrief.lede: Seven steps from a padlocked balance to the full picture of what this issuer can do, and what that means for anyone holding its token.
debrief.diagramTitle: One issuer, four customers, three powers

steps.title: A balance you can see and cannot move
steps.body: The wallet holds 10,000 tokens and a small padlock. The padlock means the issuer has taken away this wallet's permission to use that token. Nothing was moved and nothing was deleted; the balance is frozen exactly where it is.
points: The tokens arrived from the distributor in a single payment
The wallet spent part of the balance normally before the freeze, and that history is still readable
Anyone in the world can see this, including the wallet owner and their lawyer

callout.title: What this is not
callout.body: It has nothing to do with running out of XLM or losing a key. The wallet works perfectly; only that one token is blocked.

steps.title: Every question starts with the issuer
steps.body: One click on the token tile names the account that issued it. From there the token page carries the supply, the number of holders, the rules attached to the token, and whether more of it can still appear.
points: A token is a code plus an issuing account, and the code alone means nothing
The issuer publishes a website, which is a claim you can go and check
The same page tells you how many wallets hold the token

callout.title: The habit to build
callout.body: Token tile, then Issued by, then the issuer's own page. Three clicks, and you know who you are dealing with.

steps.title: Permission to hold, granted one wallet at a time
steps.body: This token was issued with approval required. A wallet that agrees to hold it still receives nothing until the issuer approves that wallet. In the history the approval arrives right after the wallet accepted the token.
points: This is how a regulated issuer keeps unverified customers out
Many bank-issued and government-linked tokens work this way; most open crypto tokens do not
The rules are chosen once, before anyone holds the token, and the token page lists them

callout.title: Read the flags first
callout.body: required, revocable and clawback_enabled are three separate powers. A token can have none of them, some of them, or all three.

steps.title: The same switch, turned off again
steps.body: Approval can be taken back at any moment, and that is the padlock. It is the most important thing to understand about a token like this: the balance is yours only while the issuer agrees that it is.
points: A frozen balance still counts towards the total supply
Nothing else about the wallet is affected; its XLM and any other tokens keep working normally
Only the issuer can undo it

callout.title: Why the power exists
callout.body: Sanctions, fraud investigations, court orders. Whether that is reassuring or alarming depends on who you are and what the token is for.

steps.title: Tokens removed without a signature
steps.body: Another customer had 5,000 tokens taken out of its wallet by the issuer. That customer signed nothing and could not have refused. The tokens were destroyed on the way out, so the supply fell.
points: The power has to be switched on before the wallet ever accepted the token
The explorer writes it in plain words: clawed back 5,000 from that wallet
This is the power that turns a token from money into a claim on a company

callout.title: Before you accept any token
callout.body: Read the flags on its page. If clawback is on, understand that somebody else holds a key to your balance.

steps.title: A supply that moves in both directions
steps.body: This issuer has issued twice, one customer sent tokens back and destroyed them, and the clawback destroyed more. The number on the token page is a snapshot, not a promise.
points: New tokens appear when the issuer sends them out, which for a bank should match new money coming in
Tokens that arrive back at the issuer stop existing and the supply drops
Compare this with mission 02, where the key was destroyed and the number can never change again

callout.title: The question to ask
callout.body: If a token claims to be worth one dollar or one dong each, the supply is the number that has to match the money held somewhere else. That is why serious issuers publish reserve reports.

steps.title: So is this a good token or a bad one?
steps.body: Neither, on its own. A bank token with approval, freezing and clawback is doing what a regulated issuer is required to do. The only real problem is a holder who did not know.
points: A fixed supply with a destroyed key, as in mission 02, is a different promise rather than a better one
What you can always check in five minutes: issuer, flags, lock status, supply, holders
What the ledger can never tell you: whether the money backing the token is really there

callout.title: Finish the homework
callout.body: Under your eight answers, write one sentence: would you accept this token as your salary, and why? There is no single right answer, but there is a wrong reason, which is not having looked.

further.title: Take it further
further.lede: Three harder questions, if you want to go past full marks.
items: The distributor is still holding most of the supply. Work out exactly how much, and what would happen to it if the issuer froze the distributor as well.
Put this token's page next to the airdrop token from mission 02 and compare the Summary boxes line by line. Write down every difference you find.
Find the moment this wallet was first approved to hold the token, and work out how long it was between that approval and the freeze.

tools.label: USDC on the real network: check its flags and compare
What Stellar is, in plain language

payments.title: Sending money across borders
payments.lede: The same 500 USD makes the same trip twice: once through the banking system, once over Stellar. Watch where it waits, who takes a cut, and how long it takes.

example.title: The example
example.body: Someone working in the US sends 500 USD to their family in Da Nang on a Friday afternoon. Every number below is an illustration, not a quote from a real bank.

wire.title: 1. How it works today
wire.lede: Banks in different countries rarely hold accounts with each other, so money hops through intermediaries while instructions travel separately over SWIFT.

steps.title: The sender goes to the bank
steps.body: They fill in the recipient's name, bank, account number and a SWIFT code. The bank checks their identity and the reason for the transfer.
points: A bank account is required on both ends
One typo in the account details and the money bounces back days later

steps.title: A message leaves, the money does not
steps.body: SWIFT only carries instructions: "pay 485 USD to this account". The money itself has to move through accounts that banks hold with each other.
points: The sending bank takes a wire fee (15 USD here)
Sent after the daily cut-off, so nothing happens until the next business day

callout.title: Message is not money
callout.body: SWIFT is like a very reliable email between banks. Settling the money is a separate job.

steps.title: An intermediary bank in the middle
steps.body: The US bank has no account in Vietnam, so a large correspondent bank that has accounts in both countries passes the money on. It takes its own fee.
points: Banks are closed over the weekend, so the money waits
Some routes need two or three intermediaries, each with a fee

steps.title: The Vietnamese bank converts to VND
steps.body: The receiving bank checks the transfer against anti money laundering rules, then converts USD to VND at its own rate, which is a little worse than the market rate.
points: The FX margin is a fee you never see on the receipt
Nobody along the way can tell the sender exactly where the money is

steps.title: The family finally gets paid
steps.body: The money lands in the family's account in VND, worth 465 USD. The sender paid 500.
points: 4 days door to door, including a weekend
35 USD, or 7 %, gone on the way

steps.title: Where the 35 USD went
steps.body: Each bank in the chain is paid for its hop, and each hop adds time. The World Bank puts the global average cost of sending money home at about 6.5 %, and above 9 % when it goes through banks.
points: Slow: days, not minutes
Expensive: several fees plus the FX margin
Opaque: no one sees the whole path

callout.title: Why so many middlemen?
callout.body: Each bank keeps its own private ledger. Moving money means every pair of banks on the route must trust and reconcile with each other.

pains.title: What is wrong with it
pains.lede: Four problems that come straight out of the diagram above.

items.title: Slow
items.body: Every hop waits for business hours and a cut-off time. Two to five days is normal.

items.title: Expensive
items.body: A fee at every bank plus a hidden FX margin. Small transfers lose the largest share.

items.title: Opaque
items.body: The sender cannot see where the money is or which fee was taken where.

items.title: Office hours only
items.body: Weekends and public holidays stop everything. Both sides also need a bank account.

fix.title: 2. What a blockchain changes
fix.lede: Three ideas, each one removing part of the chain of banks.

items.title: One shared ledger
items.body: Instead of each bank keeping its own books and reconciling, everyone reads and writes the same public ledger. Settlement takes seconds.

items.title: A digital dollar
items.body: USDC is a dollar token backed 1 : 1 by Circle (Module 1). It moves like a message, so there is no separate money leg to settle.

items.title: Anchors at the edges
items.body: An anchor is a trusted business that swaps cash for tokens and back. On Stellar, MoneyGram is one of them, with counters in 170+ countries.

moneygram.title: 3. The same 500 USD with MoneyGram on Stellar
moneygram.lede: MoneyGram lets people walk into one of its locations, pay cash, and receive USDC in a Stellar wallet, and the reverse on the other side. The middle of the trip is one Stellar payment.

steps.title: Cash in at a MoneyGram counter
steps.body: The sender opens a Stellar wallet app, chooses "deposit with MoneyGram" and pays 500 USD in cash at a nearby location. No bank account needed.
points: MoneyGram checks identity, just like a bank would
This is the anchor's job: turning cash into tokens

steps.title: USDC appears in the wallet
steps.body: MoneyGram sends USDC to the sender's wallet, minus its cash-in fee. Every USDC is backed by one real dollar at Circle, the loop from Module 1.
points: The money is now a token on a public ledger
Anyone can check the balance on Stellar Expert (Module 2)

steps.title: One payment, signed by the sender
steps.body: The wallet prepares a payment: 495 USDC to the family's address. The sender approves it, which signs it with their secret key, and the wallet sends it to the network.
points: No SWIFT code, no intermediary, no cut-off time
It works the same on a Sunday at midnight

steps.title: Settled in about 5 seconds
steps.body: Stellar validators agree on the next page of the ledger every few seconds. Once the payment is on it, it is final: nobody can reverse it or hold it for review.
points: The network fee is a tiny fraction of a cent
The family's wallet shows 495 USDC right away

callout.title: Message and money in one
callout.body: On the bank route the message and the money travel apart. Here the payment is the settlement.

steps.title: Cash out on the other side
steps.body: The family can keep USDC in the wallet, or send it to MoneyGram and pick up cash in local money at a counter. MoneyGram redeems the USDC with Circle behind the scenes.
points: The cash-out fee and FX rate are shown before confirming
The family can also just keep and spend dollars

callout.title: Depends on the country
callout.body: Cash out depends on MoneyGram locations in the receiving country. Check availability before relying on it.

steps.title: Under an hour, 12 USD
steps.body: The anchors at each end still charge for handling cash, but the expensive middle of the trip, the chain of banks, is replaced by one payment on a shared ledger.
points: Bank route: 4 days, 35 USD
MoneyGram on Stellar: under an hour, 12 USD
Every step is visible on the explorer

compare.title: Side by side
compare.lede: The same transfer, the two routes.

rows.stellar: Seconds on chain, minutes counter to counter

rows.bank: Several fees plus FX margin, about 6 to 10 %
rows.stellar: Cash in and cash out fees; the network fee is almost zero
The network runs 24/7; counters keep their own hours
No, a wallet app is enough
When the ledger closes, about 5 seconds

lifecycle.title: The life of a financial transaction
lifecycle.lede: Every payment goes through the same stages: it is created, checked, passed on, settled and confirmed. What differs is who does each stage and how long it takes.

stages.title: Create
stages.body: The sender fills in a transfer form at the bank or in its app.

stages.title: Check
stages.body: The bank verifies identity and screens for money laundering.

stages.title: Send the message
stages.body: A SWIFT message tells the next bank what to pay.

stages.title: Move the money
stages.body: Balances shift between accounts that banks hold with each other.

stages.title: Reconcile
stages.body: Each bank matches its books against the others, usually at end of day.

stages.title: Final
stages.body: Only once every bank on the route has settled.

stages.title: Create
stages.body: The wallet prepares the payment: to whom, how much, and the fee.

stages.title: Sign
stages.body: The sender approves it; the wallet signs it with the secret key.

stages.title: Submit
stages.body: The signed payment is sent to the Stellar network.

stages.title: Agree
stages.body: Validators agree on the next ledger page, about every 5 seconds.

stages.title: Record
stages.body: The payment is written to the ledger. It cannot be reversed.

stages.title: Verify
stages.body: Anyone can look it up on Stellar Expert, as you did in Module 2.

callout.title: Checking identity does not disappear
callout.body: On Stellar, the anchor (MoneyGram) still checks identity at cash in and cash out. What goes away is the chain of banks in the middle.

lending.title: Lending: the bank and Blend
lending.lede: Borrowing is the same idea everywhere: someone with spare money lends it to someone who needs it, and the borrower pledges something in case they cannot pay back. Here is who does what at a bank, and in a lending pool on Stellar.

bank.title: 1. Borrowing from a bank in Vietnam
bank.lede: Example: a 500 million VND loan secured by a house worth 1 billion. The bank sits in the middle of everything.

steps.title: Where the money comes from
steps.body: Savers deposit money and earn about 5 % a year. The bank lends that money out at a higher rate and keeps the difference.
points: Savers never know who their money was lent to
The bank decides who gets a loan and at what rate

steps.title: Paperwork and a credit check
steps.body: The borrower brings ID, proof of income and a loan purpose. The bank looks up their history at CIC, the national credit bureau.
points: No income proof or a bad CIC record usually means no loan
Many people with no credit history are left out

steps.title: The house is valued and pledged
steps.body: The bank values the house and usually lends up to about 70 % of it. The pledge is notarised and registered, and the bank keeps the house title.
points: Valuation, notary and registration take days and cost fees
The borrower keeps living in the house

steps.title: The loan is paid out
steps.body: After approval and signing the contract, the bank transfers 500 million VND to the borrower.
points: One to two weeks from application, sometimes more
Rate often fixed for a promo period, then floating

steps.title: Monthly repayments
steps.body: Each month the borrower repays part of the loan plus interest, about 10 % a year. Part of that pays the savers, the rest is the bank's margin.
points: When the loan is paid off, the bank returns the house title
Early repayment usually costs a penalty fee

steps.title: Late payments and a forced sale
steps.body: After 90 days overdue the loan becomes a bad debt, recorded at CIC. The bank can then sell the house to recover its money, a process that can take months.
points: A bad CIC record blocks future loans for years
Recovering the collateral is slow and costly for everyone

callout.title: The bank carries the trust
callout.body: Savers trust the bank, and the bank trusts its own checks. Everything depends on one institution's judgement.

idea.title: 2. A lending pool: the same job, different rules
idea.lede: In DeFi, a lending pool replaces the bank with a shared pot of money and rules everyone can read.

items.title: One shared pool
items.body: Lenders put tokens into a pool and earn interest. Borrowers take from the same pool. No bank decides who is allowed.

items.title: Collateral first, no credit check
items.body: Instead of a credit score, you deposit more value than you borrow. Your collateral is your guarantee.

items.title: Rules run by themselves
items.body: Interest rates, borrowing limits and liquidations follow fixed rules, 24/7, in seconds. Anyone can inspect them.

blend.title: 3. Blend: a lending pool on Stellar
blend.lede: Blend is the main lending protocol on Stellar. Example: a pool with USDC and XLM, where a borrower pledges 1,000 USD of XLM and borrows USDC.

steps.title: Lenders fill the pool
steps.body: People with spare USDC deposit it into the pool from their wallet. They start earning interest immediately and can withdraw whenever the money is not lent out.
points: No bank in between: lenders are the savers
Every deposit is a public transaction

steps.title: The borrower pledges XLM
steps.body: The borrower connects a wallet and supplies 1,000 USD worth of XLM as collateral. A price feed tells the pool what that XLM is worth, right now.
points: No ID papers, no income proof, no CIC check
It takes one signed transaction

steps.title: Borrow within the limit
steps.body: XLM counts for 75 % of its value in this pool, so the borrower can take up to 750 USDC. They borrow 500 and it lands in their wallet in seconds.
points: Borrowing less than the limit leaves room if prices move

callout.title: Why borrow if you already have XLM?
callout.body: To get dollars without selling your XLM, for example to pay for something while keeping your position.

steps.title: Interest set by demand
steps.body: The rate is not set by a person. The more of the pool is borrowed, the higher the rate for borrowers and the more lenders earn. A share goes to the backstop fund.
points: After 3 months the debt has grown to 510 USDC
Rates update continuously, anyone can see them

steps.title: Repay and take the XLM back
steps.body: The borrower repays 510 USDC whenever they want, then withdraws the XLM. No early repayment fee, no paperwork to release the collateral.
points: Two transactions, a few seconds each
That is the happy ending. Now, what if the price falls?

steps.title: XLM falls 35 %
steps.body: Back to the open loan of 510 USDC. XLM drops and the collateral is now worth 650 USD. Health falls below 1.00: the loan is no longer safe for lenders.
points: The borrower could have repaid part of the debt or added collateral

steps.title: A liquidator steps in
steps.body: Anyone can repay part of an unhealthy loan and receive collateral worth a bit more in return. Here a liquidator repays 310 USDC and takes about 340 USD of XLM.
points: Minutes, not months in court
The borrower keeps the 500 USDC but loses part of the XLM

callout.title: The cost of liquidation
callout.body: The discount the liquidator earns is paid by the borrower. Keeping health well above 1.00 avoids it.

steps.title: The backstop covers what is left
steps.body: If prices crash so fast that collateral cannot cover a debt, the pool's backstop fund pays the gap, so lenders are protected first.
points: Backstop depositors earn part of the interest for taking this risk
Each pool has its own backstop, so one bad pool does not sink the others

howto.title: Try it: borrowing on Blend testnet
howto.lede: Blend runs a testnet version with test tokens, so you can go through the whole loop without real money.

steps.title: Prepare Freighter
steps.body: Set it to Test Net and make sure you have test XLM, as in Module 1.

steps.title: Open Blend testnet
steps.body: Go to testnet.blend.capital and connect your Freighter wallet.

steps.title: Pick a pool
steps.body: Look at which assets it lends, the supply rate and the borrow rate.

steps.title: Supply collateral
steps.body: Supply some XLM as collateral. Freighter shows the transaction: read it, then sign.

steps.title: Borrow
steps.body: Borrow a token the pool offers. Watch your borrow limit and stay well below it.

steps.title: Repay and withdraw
steps.body: Repay the loan, withdraw your XLM, then find every step on Stellar Expert.

howto.note: Testnet only. Test tokens have no value.

compare.title: Side by side
compare.lede: Same need, two very different processes.

rows.stellar: Lenders put tokens into the pool directly

rows.bank: ID, income proof, clean CIC record, collateral
rows.stellar: A wallet and crypto collateral worth more than the loan

rows.bank: Set by the bank, promo then floating
rows.stellar: Set by supply and demand, updated continuously

rows.bank: Bad debt at CIC, house sold after months
rows.stellar: Part of the collateral liquidated within minutes
Every loan and rate is public

risks.title: It is not magic
risks.lede: A lending pool removes paperwork, not risk.
risks.calloutTitle: Know the limits before you borrow
items: You must already own assets worth more than the loan, so it does not help people with nothing to pledge.
Crypto prices move fast; a sharp drop can liquidate you in minutes.
The rules are code: a bug or a wrong price feed can cause losses.
No one to call if you make a mistake. This lesson is education, not financial advice.

sources.title: Sources
sources.lede: The Blend docs explain every rule in more detail.

issue.title: Issue your own token
issue.lede: You will create a real token on the Stellar testnet and mint the whole supply into your own wallet. Everything technical is handled for you. You choose what the token is.

wallet.title: Connect your wallet
wallet.lede: Your wallet will receive the token. It also signs one transaction: the trustline that opts you in to holding it.
wallet.notInstalledBody: Freighter is the Stellar browser wallet. Install the extension, create a wallet, then reload this page.
wallet.disconnectedBody: Connect Freighter to continue. This site can only read your public address and ask you to sign. It can never see your secret key.
wallet.wrongNetworkTitle: Freighter is on the wrong network
wallet.wrongNetworkBody: This lesson runs on the Stellar Test Net, but your wallet is on {current}. Open Freighter, use the network dropdown at the top, and choose Test Net.
wallet.unfundedTitle: This account does not exist yet
wallet.unfundedBody: A Stellar account has to be created on the ledger before it can hold anything. On testnet, Friendbot does that for free.
wallet.lowBalanceBody: Adding a trustline locks another 0.5 XLM of reserve, plus a small fee. Top up from Friendbot to be safe.

mode.title: Choose how to issue it
mode.lede: Both create a real asset on the ledger with the same code, issuer and balances. The difference is which door you open on it.

classic.name: Classic Stellar asset
classic.body: Issued with a payment operation. No contract is deployed, nothing is compiled. This is how USDC, EURC and nearly every asset on Stellar works today.
pros: Cheapest and fastest, a few thousandths of a cent per transaction
Understood by every Stellar wallet, exchange and anchor out of the box
Trades on the built-in DEX with no extra work
Compliance flags (authorize, freeze, clawback) are built into the protocol
cons: Cannot run custom logic: no fees on transfer, no vesting, no conditions
classic.bestFor: Stablecoins, tokenized deposits, points, and anything that behaves like money

sac.name: Stellar Asset Contract
sac.body: Issues the same classic asset, then deploys the built-in contract wrapper over it. The asset gets a contract address (C…) implementing the standard SEP-41 token interface, so Soroban contracts can hold and move it.
pros: Callable from smart contracts, required for DeFi, escrow, vaults
Standard token interface: transfer, approve, balance, mint, burn
Same asset, same balances, and the classic side keeps working
The contract address is derived from the asset, so it is deterministic
cons: Two extra transactions and a higher fee
Sending to a normal G-address still needs a trustline, the wrapper does not remove that
sac.bestFor: Any asset that a Soroban contract has to interact with

form.title: Describe your token
form.lede: This is the only part you actually decide. Everything after it is signed and submitted for you.
form.advancedHint: These are the flags a regulated issuer uses. Turn them on to see the extra transactions they add.

code.label: Asset code
code.hint: 1–12 letters or digits. This is the symbol wallets display. It is not unique on its own.

name.label: Token name
name.hint: The human name. On Stellar this lives off chain, in a stellar.toml file at your home domain.

description.label: Description
description.hint: Also off-chain metadata. Kept here so you can see what a real issuer would publish.
description.placeholder: A classroom token issued during the Stellar course at VKU.

supply.label: Total supply
supply.hint: Minted in full into your wallet. Maximum {max}.

homeDomain.label: Home domain
homeDomain.hint: The domain where your stellar.toml would be published. Written onto the issuing account itself.

authRequired.label: Authorization required
authRequired.hint: Holders must be approved by you before they can receive the token. This is how a regulated stablecoin enforces KYC. It adds one transaction: you authorising your own trustline.

authRevocable.label: Authorization revocable
authRevocable.hint: You can freeze a holder’s balance later. Required before clawback can be enabled.

clawbackEnabled.label: Clawback enabled
clawbackEnabled.hint: You can take the token back from any holder without their signature. Used for court orders and stolen-funds recovery, and a serious thing for a holder to accept.

lockIssuer.label: Lock the issuer afterwards
lockIssuer.hint: Sets the issuing account’s master key weight to 0 once the supply is minted. Nothing can ever be issued again: a permanent, verifiable fixed supply.

code.charset: Letters and digits only, no spaces or symbols
code.reservedXlm: XLM is the native asset. Pick another code.

supply.numeric: Digits only, with an optional decimal point
supply.range: Must be greater than 0 and at most 922,337,203,685.4775807

homeDomain.invalid: Enter a domain like vku.udn.vn, with no https:// and no path

flags.clawbackNeedsRevocable: Clawback requires “Authorization revocable” to be on

lockWarning.title: Locking is permanent
lockWarning.body: Once the issuer is locked you can never mint more, and, if you enabled them, you can never authorize a new holder, freeze anyone, or claw anything back. On testnet that costs nothing. On mainnet it is irreversible.

review.title: Check this before you sign
review.lede: Read every line. On mainnet this is the last screen before something irreversible happens, so build the habit here.
review.planLede: {count} transactions. You sign one of them; the throwaway issuer account signs the rest.

issuerNote.title: About the issuer account
issuerNote.body: A real issuer is a carefully secured account, often multisig, often in an HSM. For this lesson the app generates a throwaway testnet keypair and funds it from Friendbot, so the token can land in your own wallet where you can see it. The secret key exists only in this browser tab and is shown to you at the end.

run.title: Issuing
run.lede: Each line is one transaction on the ledger. Open any of them in the explorer.
run.signHint: Freighter is asking you to sign. Check the popup.

createIssuer.label: Create the issuer account
createIssuer.body: A fresh keypair is generated in your browser. Nothing has touched the network yet.

fundIssuer.label: Fund the issuer from Friendbot
fundIssuer.body: The account has to exist on the ledger and hold a minimum balance before it can do anything.

configureIssuer.label: Set flags and home domain
configureIssuer.body: Writes the authorization flags and the home domain onto the issuing account. Must happen before any trustline is created.

deploySac.label: Deploy the Stellar Asset Contract
deploySac.body: Creates the contract wrapper for this asset. Its address was already known, because it is derived from the asset and the network.

createTrustline.label: Your wallet opts in (trustline)
createTrustline.body: You sign this one. It records that your account accepts this asset, up to the supply, and locks 0.5 XLM of reserve.

authorizeTrustline.label: Issuer authorises your trustline
authorizeTrustline.body: Needed because you enabled “authorization required”. This is the compliance gate a regulated issuer runs for every holder.

mint.label: Mint the supply into your wallet
mint.body: The tokens come into existence as they leave the issuing account.

mintSac.label: Mint through the contract
mintSac.body: Calls mint() on the Stellar Asset Contract. The issuing account is the contract’s admin, so its signature is the authorisation.

lockIssuer.label: Lock the issuer
lockIssuer.body: Sets the master key weight to 0. The supply is now fixed forever, and anyone can verify that on the ledger.

run.failedTitle: That step did not go through
run.failedBody: Nothing before it was undone. Fix the cause and continue. The flow picks up from here.

result.title: Your token exists
result.lede: It is on the Stellar testnet ledger, and the supply is in your wallet. Open Freighter and look.
result.lockedNo: Issuer unlocked, more can be minted
result.secretBody: This is the key that can mint more of your token. It was generated in this browser tab and is not stored anywhere. Close the tab and it is gone forever. On mainnet, a key like this would be the single most valuable secret your company owns.
learned: You created an ordinary Stellar account and it became an issuer the moment it sent its first payment
Your wallet had to opt in with a trustline before it could receive anything, and 0.5 XLM of yours is now locked behind it
The supply is not stored anywhere: it is the sum of every holder’s balance, and it grew when the tokens left the issuer
Everything you just did is what Circle does for USDC, at a different scale and with dollars behind it
try: Open the asset in the explorer and find the holder count. It should be 1, you
Send some of it to a classmate. They will have to add a trustline first, and you will watch it fail if they do not
Issue the same code again from a different issuer, and see why wallets show the issuer and not just the symbol
If you locked the issuer, try issuing more. The ledger will refuse, and that is what makes a fixed supply credible
